lesson_title: Sell the Chocolate, Not the Beans
hook_text: A cocoa farmer earns a few rand per kilogram. The same kilogram sells for hundreds in a mall. Where did the money go?
clip_script: Put one street in your head with a spaza shop at one end and a giant supermarket at the other. The spaza sells what it can gather cheaply — loose oranges, bundles of firewood. The supermarket sells processed goods — bread, data, medicine — and the profit hides in the processing. Watch the money: the spaza owner sells cheap raw things and buys expensive processed things, day after day, and the money drifts up the street in one direction only. That street is the world economy in miniature. A cocoa farmer earns a few rand on a kilogram of beans; the same kilogram, processed into slabs and branded, sells for hundreds in a mall. The difference — the value added — settles where the processing happens, never where the pod was picked. Now the swap rate. This year one bag of oranges swaps for one phone. Next season, phone prices climb while orange prices sag — the same phone costs FOUR bags. You planted more, picked more, shipped more, and can afford less. That is deteriorating terms of trade, and you did nothing to deserve it. South Africa works both ends of the street: platinum and coal out spaza-style, finished cars from Kariega and Durban out supermarket-style. The whole game of trade policy in one line — stop selling only the beans; start selling the chocolate.
visual_style: A single street morphing between a spaza counter and supermarket aisles; animated rand notes drifting one way up the street; a scale weighing bags of oranges against one phone as the bags multiply; a container ship loading ore on one side and finished cars on the other.
mood: Sharp and revealing, ending with strategic optimism.
pacing: Easy street-scene open, tightening on the four-bags reveal, punchy chocolate-line close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and argue world trade from either side.
